body:
I think that something along these lines could serve more broadly as a Starship health-check tool for troubleshooting: printing ASCII, Unicode, emoji, powerline and nerd font icons to confirm that everything is wired up correctly.

I'd be in favor of having this as a top-level command rather than a module. It something along the lines of `starship debug`.

I don't think this is like `brew doctor` as it can't find any issues and so can't suggest possible fixes. It's more like a preview, as it shows some of what starship is capable of displaying and how it will come out in the current environment. Though I wouldn't use that name as it sounds like what `starship prompt` does. I think `starship preflight` could work, but I also don't have a problem with `starship debug`.

> One challenge is that starship is unable to tell whether the symbols have printed correctly, so it is up to the user to examine the output and make sure things make sense. That needs to be communicated in the output somehow.

Do you mean more than making the format match the style? As in my example `[lightgrey](lightgrey)`. If not can you clarify? If this was extended to also print a sample of unusual or problematic graphemes (which I do support) then I would think this would print its character name alongside e.g. `[:rocket: \U0001f680 ]('')`

> @ucodery For colors, was there any particular set you were thinking of?

Thanks for bringing this point up. I was thinking about this problem myself as it is feasibly impractical to print every RGB color, let alone the combination of fg bg. There are similarly too many graphemes in the unicode standard to attempt every one.

For my own purposes I just wanted something that would print out the basic named colors plus all colors I have defined in my custom palette. I'm unsure if I had multiple palettes if I would want non-activated ones to also show up. But I would like to permutate these values with the `dimmed` and `inverted` styles. I think that, practically, I am not going to use color values that I have not assigned to a name, especially if I am working with a palette. However, I do recognize that as debug output this may not be very helpful. For one these names probably don't cover a well distributed selection of the available colors, and for another any custom names would have to be printed along with their table values to be of any use to another developer, as would be necessary for bug reports.

To be a useful debug output whatever colors are output should probably be combined with all of the style string words except `bg:` `fg:` (it would be too many, and not always readable; but some select number of backgrounds should probably be tried) and `blink` (IMO this should be off by default and enabled with a switch. I don't want blinding marque text popping up when I am debugging, and as noted in the docs it would just repeat plain text on many terminals anyways).

> (e.g. evaluate all possible modules, look at their colors, and then display the union of all those?)
Off-topic, is it possible that color names can be added that aren't terminal named colors or defined in a palette? As a user I was not aware of this.

For text debug output I would start very small selection and increase as needed with issues or PRs. I thing that even the entire printable range of ASCII is too much, I would rather see a very few selected characters from major unicode groups, and nerdfonts, be chosen. E.g. 2-4 each from `Latin1` `Katakana` `Arabic` `Mathmatical Operatinos` `Box Drawing` `Braille Patterns` `Emoticons`

If `starship debug` is what this ends up being called, how should the interface be set up?

I think that without further arguments or options it should output a sting that is most useful too copy or screenshot for new issues. So whatever is most helpful to the maintinaers, trying to not scroll output off of a typical terminal size.

I think it would make sense to then have subcommands like the original module suggestion. So `starship debug color`, `starship debug nerdfonts` `starship debug powerline`. I could see more options being added like `starship debug color palette.mypalette` or `starship debug color --underline --inverted` or maybe a verbose/ terse flag that applies equally well to any. But this might be over-engineering a command that doesn't even exist yet.

Also, I wonder if `starship bug-report` should be updated to include this output, but is it really helpful as not-a-screenshot?

> Do you mean more than making the format match the style? As in my example [lightgrey](lightgrey). If not can you clarify?

I think we're on the same page here. I was just pointing out that unlike `brew doctor`, `starship` is unable to report when things haven't rendered properly, so `doctor` is probably not a good name for it. 

> Off-topic, is it possible that color names can be added that aren't terminal named colors or defined in a palette? As a user I was not aware of this.

I don't think it is. I was referring to the fact that some modules use a hardcoded RGB hex as their default color, so iterating the named colors and palette colors won't necessarily give you all the colors that could show up in a default config. On the flipside, the probability that someone wants to debug a default hardcoded color seems pretty low.

> I think that without further arguments or options it should output a sting that is most useful too copy or screenshot for new issues. So whatever is most helpful to the maintinaers, trying to not scroll output off of a typical terminal size.

This sounds reasonable. Some short collection of default colors (probably not even palettes, since those are more advanced), and a few representative glyphs from each font. We can probably target a standard terminal size (say, 80x35 characters).

> I think it would make sense to then have subcommands like the original module suggestion.

I agree. Off the top of my head, I think we want at least `colors` and `fonts`. I don't think indexing too far into fonts at the first subcommand level is a good idea (a lot of our users don't know the difference between emoji and nerdfont, nevermind the finer distinction between symbols in the nerdfont category).

> Also, I wonder if starship bug-report should be updated to include this output, but is it really helpful as not-a-screenshot?

I don't think that helps. You'll get the same binary stream that the terminal spits out, so even if it makes it into the browser, you're just testing whether the person viewing the bug report has nerdfont/powerline/emoji rendering available in their browser, instead of what the user is seeing in their terminal.
